name: Continuous-wire papermaking and reeling
summary: A machine that made paper as one endless sheet on a moving wire mesh instead of sheet by sheet by hand, greatly increasing how much paper a mill could produce.
description: Mechanized papermaking in which pulp drains on a moving continuous wire, passes through presses, and is wound as a continuous web before cutting and drying.
tier_reason: Continuous sheet production supports subsequent printing, packaging and administrative infrastructure over generations.

impact.note: Papermaking was reorganised around the machine and cheap paper spread across continents, founding one industrial line; generativity 2 implies tier 1, not the reviewed tier 0.

why: Robert's French prototype rights were brought to England, where the Fourdrinier stationers financed its development into a commercial machine.

earliest_record.rationale: Earliest defensible dated record of this scoped referent in the retained evidence; later community entry is recorded separately. The trade-association report says commercial operation in 1803, while Krebs places the commercial machine in 1804. Historical accounts differ between 1803 and 1804 and may describe successive machines; the one-sided bound does not settle worldwide priority or exact first operation. This is the earliest supported record currently established here, not certification of absolute priority.

community_entry.community: Frogmore mill workers making machine-produced paper
community_entry.rationale: Commercial operation at Frogmore by the later of the conflicting 1803 and 1804 dates reaches a working papermaking community. It is not the invention of Robert’s earlier prototype.
community_entry.proxy_reason: The operator and historical accounts document commercial operation at the mill, but disagree over the early machine’s year and individual commissioning.
community_entry.caveats: Historical accounts differ between 1803 and 1804 and may describe successive machines; the one-sided bound does not settle worldwide priority or exact first operation.

caveats: Robert’s continuous-wire prototype in France preceded the Frogmore plant; cited histories differ between 1803 and 1804 for commercial Frogmore operation. Global first commercial use remains unproven.

links.statement: The Frogmore account describes continuous-wire papermaking as mechanising elements of hand papermaking: fibre pulp is drained, pressed and formed into paper in a continuous moving web.
links.scope: The general paper-forming process and the Frogmore account of a later industrial machine; no specific ancient fragment is linked directly to the mill.
links.alternatives: Continuous machines modify furnish, mechanical formation and finishing; the relationship does not claim unchanged recipes or universal preservation of every hand process.
links.caveats: The local source describes the machine as a version of papermaking by hand but does not establish a direct chain from Xuanquanzhi or Hantanpo to Frogmore.
links.timing: The cited Han witnesses and the Frogmore machine are separated by many centuries; this is a documented functional adaptation, not an uninterrupted or direct transmission claim.

evidence.locator: Machine description, comparison with hand papermaking
evidence.supports: Frogmore’s account explicitly compares the machine’s pulp formation and subsequent finishing with manual papermaking.

evidence.locator: English abstract: inferred mould-forming of early fibre sheets
evidence.supports: The archaeological study identifies early manually formed fibre-sheet examples, without tracing a lineage to the machine.

unresolved.note: Frogmore No. 2 shut down while the distinct pilot was observed operating in 2013. The end of continuous-wire papermaking is not established.
